name: Little League elbow
aliases: medial elbow overuse injury in throwers

clinicalPearls: A spectrum of overuse injury to the medial elbow in skeletally immature throwing athletes, centred on the medial epicondyle apophysis
Repetitive valgus stress during the throwing motion causes traction injury at the medial epicondyle
Presents with medial elbow pain during and after throwing, sometimes with reduced throwing velocity and control
Severe cases can produce avulsion of the medial epicondyle apophysis
It is strongly linked to excessive pitching volume, and pitch-count and rest guidelines are central to prevention
Management is relative rest from throwing, mechanics correction and graded return, with surgery for significant displaced avulsion
reference.pathophysiology: Little League elbow results from repetitive valgus forces generated during overhead throwing, which place traction on the medial structures of the immature elbow, particularly the medial epicondyle apophysis where the flexor-pronator muscles and ulnar collateral ligament attach. The growth cartilage is weaker than the adjacent tendon and ligament, so repetitive stress causes apophysitis and, when overload is severe, apophyseal separation or avulsion. Lateral compressive forces can additionally injure the capitellum in the same throwing mechanism.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of medial elbow tenderness and throwing history
Radiographs, including comparison views, for apophyseal widening or avulsion
MRI where soft-tissue or osteochondral injury is suspected
Assessment of throwing mechanics and workload
redFlags: Locking or mechanical symptoms suggesting osteochondritis dissecans with loose bodies
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and rest most young throwers recover fully, but continued overload risks apophyseal avulsion and longer-term elbow problems; adherence to workload limits is protective.
pitfalls: Missing capitellar osteochondritis dissecans as a coexisting lateral injury
Overlooking a displaced avulsion needing surgery
Not addressing pitch counts and throwing mechanics
management: Institute relative rest with cessation of throwing until symptom-free, the mainstay of management
Provide analgesia and ice for the medial epicondyle apophysitis
Correct throwing mechanics and enforce pitch-count and rest guidelines to prevent recurrence
Deliver physiotherapy for flexor-pronator and shoulder-girdle strengthening before a graded, staged return to throwing
Undertake surgical fixation for significantly displaced medial epicondyle avulsion
Follow the apophysis radiographically and assess ulnar nerve function
Educate the athlete, family and coaches on workload limits and early reporting of pain
